problem: The sign is wrong under the chapter's own convention. The main equation is h₁ + v₁²/2 + gz₁ + q = h₂ + v₂²/2 + gz₂ + w_s, where w_s is defined as shaft work done by the fluid. Setting q = 0 and dropping kinetic and potential terms gives h₁ = h₂ + w_s, so w_s = h₁ − h₂. The book prints w_s = h₂ − h₁, which is the sign of the work done on the fluid and contradicts the definition just above it.
fix: Adiabatic compressor or turbine with small velocity change: w_s = h₁ − h₂ per kg. This is positive for a turbine (work leaves) and negative for a compressor (work enters). The work put into a compressor is h₂ − h₁.

where: Section 3, first paragraph after the P formula
problem: "For compression h₂ is larger than h₁, so w_s is positive: work is done on the fluid." With w_s defined as work done by the fluid, h₂ > h₁ makes w_s negative, not positive. A student who follows this sentence will write the wrong sign in the energy equation, and it directly contradicts the Section 1 bullet that says w_s = h₂ − h₁.
fix: For compression h₂ > h₁, so w_s = h₁ − h₂ is negative: work is done on the fluid, and the input per kg is the positive quantity h₂ − h₁, which is what P = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) measures. A turbine reverses this: h₂ < h₁, w_s is positive, and work leaves with the shaft.

problem: The units do not match the working. Section 3 says h₁ and h₂ are in J/kg and P comes out in W, to be divided by 1000 for kW. Quiz Q3 then puts kJ/kg values (350 − 290 = 60) straight into P = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) and calls 0.5 × 60 = 30 kW, with no conversion. Taken with J/kg as stated, the same numbers give 30 W. In a chapter whose lead warns about exactly this unit slip, the two procedures must agree.
fix: Choose one set of units and keep it. Either state h in kJ/kg, so P = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) is already in kW (kg/s × kJ/kg = kW), and delete the "divide by 1000" line; or keep h in J/kg, P in W, and show the conversion in Q3: P = 0.5 × 60 000 = 30 000 W = 30 kW.

problem: "For compression h₂ > h₁, so the work term is positive work done on the fluid" repeats the sign muddle of Section 3 while the trap is about the sign. Written as it stands, the trap teaches the wrong rule.
fix: Reversing the compressor sign. In the equation w_s is work done by the fluid, so for compression h₂ > h₁ and w_s = h₁ − h₂ is negative; the work input per kg is h₂ − h₁. For a turbine h₂ < h₁, w_s is positive and work leaves.

problem: The conclusion (lower exit velocity) is right, but the reason is self-contradictory: "less energy is available for kinetic energy at the same exit enthalpy" followed by "The exit enthalpy is also slightly lower". The exit enthalpy is not the same in the two cases, and the phrase will confuse a student trying to set up the comparison.
fix: State it in two clean steps. Heat leaves the fluid, so the equation gives v₂²/2 = h₁ − h₂ + v₁²/2 − q_out, and the q_out term reduces the exit kinetic energy. At the same exit pressure the cooled gas also has a lower exit enthalpy (lower entropy at that pressure), so the enthalpy drop is slightly larger; that partly offsets the loss but does not cancel it, and the velocity is still lower than in the adiabatic case.

problem: "A nozzle is a duct whose cross-section narrows, so the fluid speeds up" is only the subsonic picture. Section 4 and quiz Q6 both deal with gas velocities of 400 m/s and the throat, where the accelerating part of the nozzle widens. A student can read the two sections as contradicting each other.
fix: Add one clause: in a gas nozzle the flow speeds up in the converging part and, once the throat is sonic, also in a diverging part; the simple statement holds for liquids and for slow gas flow.

problem: "Compressible flow becomes hard when velocity approaches the speed of sound; the flow behaviour there needs the second law" is too vague to teach anything. Choking follows from mass, energy and the sonic condition; the second law is what rules out processes and fixes the isentropic limit.
fix: Say instead: near the speed of sound the area–velocity relation reverses (mass conservation with ρ falling faster than v rises), and the second law decides which exit states are possible, so the ideal limit is an isentropic expansion.
